content: The section discusses the treatment of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) and pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (pre-XDR-TB) using various regimens, including the novel BPaLM regimen. MDR/RR-TB has become a significant global health challenge due to poor management of drug-susceptible TB and the transmission of drug-resistant strains. While MDR/RR-TB is treatable, the regimens are often lengthy, toxic, and complex, necessitating the development of shorter, safer, and more effective treatment options. In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended a standardized 9-month regimen containing injectable agents based on observational studies in Asia and Africa. This was a significant reduction compared to the previous 18–20-month regimens. By 2018, modifications were made to this regimen, replacing kanamycin with amikacin due to evidence of better safety and effectiveness. However, the toxicity of injectable agents led to further advancements, including the development of all-oral, shorter regimens. South Africa provided observational data on a 9-month all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline, which WHO reviewed and recommended in 2019. This regimen included a combination of bedaquiline, levofloxacin (or moxifloxacin), ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. In 2022, further evidence from South Africa led to a modification of this regimen, replacing ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid. The BPaL regimen, consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, was evaluated in the Nix-TB study for its safety and effectiveness in treating MDR/RR-TB with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. While the study showed promising results, limitations such as small sample sizes, lack of blinding, and early trial termination prevented WHO from recommending its widespread use. Instead, the BPaL regimen was recommended for use under operational research conditions in the 2020 WHO guidelines. Two randomized controlled trials, TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix, completed in 2021, provided new evidence prompting WHO to reassess and update its recommendations. The BPaLM regimen offers several advantages, including shorter treatment duration, reduced pill burden, and lower costs due to fewer outpatient visits, inpatient stays, and laboratory tests. These factors make it a cost-effective and potentially equitable option, particularly in underserved settings. However, challenges such as drug availability, the need for drug susceptibility testing, and safety monitoring remain barriers to implementation. The WHO panel judged the BPaLM regimen to have large desirable effects, minimal undesirable effects, and moderate-to-large cost savings. While the certainty of evidence was rated very low due to study limitations, the panel concluded that the benefits of the BPaLM regimen likely outweigh the risks and costs, making it a favorable option for MDR/RR-TB treatment. The panel also noted that the regimen is likely acceptable to patients and healthcare providers and feasible to implement in most settings.
